clue.text: Not that their drivers are necessarily puffed up

definitions.text: Not that their drivers are necessarily puffed up

parts.words: Not that their drivers are necessarily puffed up
parts.note: the drivers are railway engine drivers; it is the machines, not the men, that are puffed up with vapour

explanation.surface: A remark that certain drivers are not always conceited.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Puffed up' reads as vain, but here it means blown along by vapour: these engines puff, whatever their drivers are like.
explanation.definitionFit: Locomotives powered by boiling water are driven by men who need not be vain, though the machines themselves puff.

clue.text: But no hammer-blows when these occur in the foundry

definitions.text: But no hammer-blows when these occur in the foundry

parts.words: But no hammer-blows when these occur in the foundry
parts.note: hammer-blows are knocks, but the knocks meant here are workers' stoppages, when nobody hammers

explanation.surface: An observation that the foundry falls quiet at certain times.
explanation.walkthrough: The word means blows, but also walkouts by workers; during those, no hammers fall.
explanation.definitionFit: Industrial walkouts by workers share the word for blows with a hammer.

parts.note: Chopin wrote two sets of piano studies, known by the French word for a study

explanation.surface: An invitation to take lessons from the composer Chopin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Study with' reads as 'learn from', but it means a study as Chopin would call it, in French.
explanation.definitionFit: The French word for a study is used for piano exercises, Chopin's most famous being his two sets.

parts.note: the night-time fairyland is Shakespeare's 'A ... Night's Dream', set at the June solstice

explanation.surface: A description of a fairy-tale night at the turn of the year.
explanation.walkthrough: The solstice is the summer one, and the night of fairies is Shakespeare's play about that night.
explanation.definitionFit: The longest-day festival in June gives its name to Shakespeare's comedy of fairies in a wood at night.

parts.note: Wilkie Collins wrote a novel called 'No ...', so 'No title' completes the book's own title

explanation.surface: A complaint that a Victorian novelist's book lacked a title.
explanation.walkthrough: Collins's 1862 novel is 'No Name': a title is a name, so 'No title' is itself the book.
explanation.definitionFit: A title is what something is called, and Collins's novel about illegitimacy is called 'No Name'.

parts.note: the last line of Matthew Arnold's poem 'Dover Beach', with its adjective left out

explanation.surface: A gapped quotation from Matthew Arnold's poem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dover Beach' ends 'And we are here as on a darkling plain ... Where ignorant armies clash by night.'
explanation.definitionFit: Arnold's armies are unknowing, fighting blind in the dark, which is the adjective of the line.

parts.note: Milton's 'Lycidas' has 'the rathe primrose that forsaken dies'; rathe means early, and a primrose springs from the ground

explanation.surface: A question about where Milton's early primrose comes from.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rathe' is an old word for early-blooming; the flower grows from the soil.
explanation.definitionFit: Flowers spring from the soil, the ground in which they grow.

explanation.surface: Biblical Joseph seen as a case for psychoanalysis.
explanation.walkthrough: In Genesis Joseph's brothers mock him as 'this dreamer'; Freud's great work interpreted dreams, so the sleeper who has them is his subject.
explanation.definitionFit: Genesis calls Joseph a seer of visions in sleep, and Freud studied the people who have such visions.

clue.text: Burlington House chief and I render a laudatory vocal duet

parts.note: Burlington House is the home of the Royal Academy, headed by its President, abbreviated PRA
to render a song is to perform it, to sing

explanation.surface: The head of the Royal Academy joins the speaker in a two-part song of praise.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'vocal duet' is the President and 'I' singing together; Burlington House in London's Piccadilly houses the Royal Academy of Arts.
explanation.definitionFit: Laudatory words are complimentary ones, expressing admiration.

parts.note: a golfer plays rounds, so he is a man of rounds; a tradesman who calls round collecting customers' orders bears the same title

explanation.surface: A golfer seems to be accepting instructions on the course.
explanation.walkthrough: A golfer 'plays a round', making him a round's man; the real word is the delivery man who goes round taking orders.
explanation.definitionFit: A roundsman is a tradesman's employee who calls at houses on a regular route, taking and delivering orders.

parts.note: before television came the peep show carried round fairs, a box of pictures viewed through a hole, called by this name with 'show' added

explanation.surface: A question about what came before television entertainment.
explanation.walkthrough: The word completes 'raree show', the travelling peep show of old fairs, which like television showed pictures in a box.
explanation.definitionFit: A raree show was a portable peep-show box of pictures, an early ancestor of screen entertainment.

parts.note: a keep is the strongest tower of a castle
something erected is put up, standing upright

explanation.surface: A fortress has been built, keeping pace with the neighbours.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on the idiom 'keep up with the Joneses', matching one's neighbours' spending.
explanation.definitionFit: To match the neighbours' lifestyle is to maintain pace with them, the idiom about the Joneses.

clue.text: There is a charm about this kind of antiquity

indicators.note: about here means moved around, so the letters of the words before it are rearranged

explanation.surface: A remark that old things have a certain charm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like 'concerning', but it is the anagram signal for IS A CHARM.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaism is an old-fashioned word or usage, a piece of linguistic antiquity kept alive.

parts.note: a line from Thomas Gray's 'Ode on the Death of a Favourite Cat', describing the cat that drowned in a tub of goldfish

explanation.surface: Praise for the most modest of striped cats.
explanation.walkthrough: Gray's ode runs 'Demurest of the tabby kind, The pensive ... reclined': the missing word is the cat's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Selima was Horace Walpole's cat, named in Gray's poem as the demure tabby who drowned.

clue.text: His pride is in his garden !

definitions.text: His pride is in his garden !

parts.words: His pride is in his garden !
parts.note: London pride is a pink-flowered saxifrage, so a resident of the capital keeps his own 'pride' growing in the garden

explanation.surface: A gardener boasting of his flowerbeds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pride' reads as self-esteem, but London pride is a common British garden plant, a saxifrage.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of the capital would naturally grow London pride, the flower named for his city.

clue.text: A broken fire-iron is not' so good

indicators.note: something broken is in pieces, so the letters of the poker are rearranged

explanation.surface: A damaged poker is of lesser quality.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broken' rearranges the eight letters of FIRE-IRON.
explanation.definitionFit: Something of lower quality or worse is described as lesser, below standard.

clue.text: Issue that gives me back a race

indicators.note: given back means turned round, so the word me is written in reverse

parts.note: a race of people is a nation

explanation.surface: Something that produces a returning racial group.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' reverses ME to EM.
explanation.definitionFit: An issue is something that flows or comes out from a source, an outpouring.

parts.note: in 'Through the Looking-Glass', Tweedledum arms for battle wearing a kitchen pot on his head

explanation.surface: A question about the headgear of Lewis Carroll's character.
explanation.walkthrough: In Carroll's book Alice helps Tweedledum dress for his fight, and he puts a cooking pot on as his helmet.
explanation.definitionFit: Tweedledum's makeshift helmet was a kitchen pot with a handle, used for boiling.

parts.note: Samuel Butler's poem 'A Psalm of ...' has the refrain 'O God! O ...!', so the gap is the Canadian city

explanation.surface: A quotation with a gap from the Victorian writer Samuel Butler.
explanation.walkthrough: Butler's poem mocks a Canadian museum that hid a cast of the Discobolus; each verse ends with the cry naming the city.
explanation.definitionFit: The refrain of Butler's satirical poem invokes the Canadian city where he saw the statue hidden away.

parts.note: Mercator was the Flemish cartographer of the famous projection, so what his pen did was chart the world

explanation.surface: A question about the writing instrument of the mapmaker Mercator.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pen' looks like the instrument, but means what Mercator did with it: draw charts.
explanation.definitionFit: Mercator's work was cartography, drawing charts of the globe.

explanation.surface: An exclamation at a heap of seaweed.
explanation.walkthrough: The word means both a confused knot and a kind of large brown seaweed, kelp.
explanation.definitionFit: A mass of knotted things is a snarl, and a large kelp found on shores carries the same name.

clue.text: Needed roughly about a thousand to put one right

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the shuffled letters go around the next piece
roughly means in a rough, disordered way, so the letters of the word before it are rearranged

parts.note: M is the Roman numeral for a thousand

explanation.surface: Something was needed for about a thousand to set one straight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roughly' rearranges NEEDED to EMENDED-less-M, and 'about' puts those letters around M; 'one' in the definition is a text being corrected.
explanation.definitionFit: To correct a text by removing errors is to amend it, as an editor does.

clue.text: But its Archbishop isn't necessarily without capital

definitions.text: But its Archbishop isn't necessarily without capital

parts.words: But its Archbishop isn't necessarily without capital
parts.note: an archbishop presides over an ecclesiastical region; such a region, though its name also means the country outside the capital, has its own seat

explanation.surface: A remark that a certain archbishop is not short of money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without capital' suggests penniless, but it means away from the capital city: the regions are outside it, yet an archbishop's region has a cathedral city.
explanation.definitionFit: An archbishop's jurisdiction is called by the same word as the country regions outside the capital.

clue.text: Behold. I depart out of it — into the blizzard ?

definitions.text: Behold. I depart out of it — into the blizzard ?

indicators.note: I and depart are said to be outside it, so they wrap around the word for behold

parts.note: to depart is to go
lo is an old word meaning behold

explanation.surface: A traveller announcing departure from a shelter into a snowstorm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of it' places I GO outside LO; the whole clue describes leaving a snow-house for the storm.
explanation.definitionFit: An Inuit snow-house is what one would leave to step out into a blizzard.

parts.note: a grey horse marked with rounded patches is called a 'grey' of this kind, and the word also means to mark with spots

explanation.surface: An invitation to pick out the grey horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spot' reads as 'notice', but it is the verb to mark with spots; a spotted grey horse is a '... grey'.
explanation.definitionFit: To mottle with patches is to fleck, and a grey horse with darker rounded markings has that name.

parts.note: Longleat is an English stately home with a safari park of lions; Jane Austen's novel title gives the word for a group of lions

explanation.surface: A question about what Jane Austen gave to a stately home.
explanation.walkthrough: Austen wrote 'Pride and Prejudice'; Longleat, a stately home in Wiltshire, has a famous safari park whose lions form a pride.
explanation.definitionFit: A group of lions, as kept at Longleat's safari park, shares its name with the first word of Austen's novel.

parts.note: legend says the Greek philosopher Empedocles threw himself into the crater of the Sicilian volcano

explanation.surface: A question about where a Greek philosopher was cremated.
explanation.walkthrough: Empedocles is said to have leapt into the Sicilian volcano to prove himself immortal, leaving only a sandal behind.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sicilian volcano into which Empedocles leapt served as his funeral fire.

clue.text: My turn for the hand-out; that's perfect

parts.note: the speaker says 'my', so the word for oneself, I, is used
handing out the cards is to deal

explanation.surface: A card player pleased that it is their go to deal.
explanation.walkthrough: At cards 'my turn to hand out' is 'I deal'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something perfect is flawless, the best one could imagine.

clue.text: Hard effect of looking at a jelly-fish ?

definitions.text: Hard effect of looking at a jelly-fish ?

parts.words: Hard effect of looking at a jelly-fish ?
parts.note: a jelly-fish is also called a medusa, and looking at the Gorgon Medusa turned people to stone

explanation.surface: A question about what happens if you stare at a sea creature.
explanation.walkthrough: The jelly-fish is a medusa; in myth, anyone who looked at Medusa was turned to stone, made hard.
explanation.definitionFit: Being turned to stone is the myth's fate for those who met Medusa's gaze; the word also means terrified.

parts.note: the jet is one of water, and the source of a water jet is a spring or the head of a fountain

explanation.surface: A history-of-engineering question about who invented the jet engine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jet propulsion' suggests aircraft, but the jet is a jet of water, which starts at its spring.
explanation.definitionFit: A spring or source of water is where a jet starts, and the word also means any origin.
